title: Failure Handling & Model Selection
subtitle: retriable vs terminal, tiers by eval

beats.narration: Your trace now points at the failing step. Next question: what does the system do the moment a failure happens in live traffic? Production throws failures development never shows you, and the difference between resilient and fragile is whether you decided in advance what each one gets.

elements.text: decide each failure's fate IN ADVANCE

beats.narration: Every failure starts with a single question: would waiting and retrying the exact same request plausibly work? If yes, it's retriable — a rate limit clears, an overload passes, a dropped connection comes back. If no, it's terminal — a malformed request fails identically forever, and an expired key doesn't heal. On the API, the status code sorts the bucket for you. And when you're unsure, default to terminal: a failure wrongly marked terminal fails loudly and gets fixed. Wrongly marked retriable, it hammers the service and hides the real problem behind a wall of retries.

elements.text:
would waiting help?
yes → retriable · no → terminal

unsure? default TERMINAL —
loud beats hidden behind retries

beats.narration: Two refinements before you write a retry loop. First, the SDK already retries transient failures with progressive delays. Stacking your own loop on top multiplies attempts against the same rate limit — decide where the retry lives, and let exactly one layer own it. Second, a rate-limited response usually includes a retry-after value telling you exactly when capacity returns. Honor it first, and fall back to exponential backoff with jitter only when the header is absent.

elements.text: before you write a retry loop

items.text: the SDK already retries — don't stack loops
exactly ONE layer owns the retry
honor retry-after · backoff is the fallback

beats.narration: When a tool your code runs fails, return the error to the model with the error flag set — never a silent empty result. With the flag, the model can react: try another approach, ask, or stop. Without it, the model treats emptiness as valid data and builds a confident wrong answer on top. One more case the status code won't catch: a refusal arrives as a successful response with a refusal stop reason. That's a content decision, not a transient fault. Raise it, log it, never blind-retry it.

elements.text:
refusal = a 200 with stop_reason "refusal"
→ fail fast, log, never blind-retry

beats.narration: Now the classic. A developer called the API in a loop with no error path, because development had never failed. At the first traffic peak, the first rate-limit response took the whole request down. The instinct fix — instant retries in a tight loop — made it worse: every immediate retry counted against the same limit and deepened it. The real fix is everything above. Classify it retriable, back off exponentially with a cap, and honor retry-after when the response offers one. Development never produces this failure. You write the path before traffic finds the gap.

elements.text: watch out: the call that never failed in dev

instant retries = more requests
against the SAME limit

beats.narration: Part two of this section: choosing the model, because that choice sets the budget everything else optimizes within. Claude is a family of tiers trading cost, latency, and capability, and the same prompt runs on any of them. The discipline: start with the balanced default. Step up a tier only when your eval shows it missing the bar on the hardest cases and a wrong answer is expensive. Step down only when the eval shows the cheaper model still holding the bar. In both directions the eval is the gate, never vibes.

items.text: step UP: eval misses the bar + mistakes are costly
step DOWN: eval shows the bar still holds

elements.text: the eval is the gate — not vibes

beats.narration: And for mixed traffic, the router idea returns, applied to models: a balanced default plus an override on a cheap signal — task type, input length, difficulty. You pay for the big model only on the requests that need it. Uniform traffic? Pin one model and skip the router.

elements.code:
default:  balanced tier      (bulk of traffic)
override: top tier           (hard cases only)
signal:   task type · length · difficulty

elements.text: pay for the big model only where it's needed
✓ uniform traffic → pin one model, no router

beats.narration: The reflex: sort every failure into retriable or terminal before traffic does it for you, and let the eval, not the price sheet, pick the tier. Two checkpoints follow — repair a broken retry loop, and choose models for three scenarios. One debrief covers both. Then: cost and orchestration.

elements.text:
sort failures in advance ·
let the eval pick the tier
